podcast.body: Bits of the piano sound in Oasis' "Don't Look Back In Anger" are said to be similar to those in John Lennon's "Imagine." "Plus, the bits of the piano sound sort of similar to Lenin's Imagine."

podcast.body: Released a year after George Harrison's "My Sweet Lord," this song asks listeners to envision a peaceful world without heaven or religion. Following his death, Yoko Ono was repeatedly asked to permit changing the lyric to "one religion" instead of "no religion," but she consistently refused, adhering to the song's message that "one religion is not better than another." "John Lennon released Imagine, which asks us to imagine a peaceful world, imagine there is no heaven, no religion to"

podcast.body: Released on October 11th, 1971, this song became a single in the United States three months after the 26th Amendment was certified, reaching number three on the Billboard charts. It emerged as another global anthem for peace and was inspired by Yoko Ono's poetry from her 1964 book *Grapefruit*. While Lennon initially took sole songwriting credit, Yoko Ono finally received credit 48 years later in 2017. "In the middle of the night, imagine all the people living for today. Imagine there's no country, it isn't hard to do."

podcast.body: This song was written and released by John Lennon in 1971, after the tragic shootings at Kent State University. Its message of unity resonated deeply with audiences in the wake of such events. "Now John Lennon wrote and released Imagine after the shootings in 1971, so you can see why the messaging about unity would resonate."
